posts.text:
The Federal Reserve held its federal funds target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on October 28, 2026, in a 10 to 2 vote.

The Fed does not set the prime rate. Individual banks do, and many base it partly on that target. The Fed's H.15 release shows prime at 7.00 percent on October 29, 2026.

Illustrative: prime plus 1.5 is 8.50 percent. On $520,000 interest-only, that is $3,683.33 a month. Each quarter point of change moves it $108.33.

Prime did not move, so neither did that payment. Lenders can check the note for the index and adjustment date.

posts.text:
Is bank money getting easier or harder for construction and land deals? The Fed asked loan officers.

In the survey released May 4, 2026, covering the first quarter, 61 banks answered on construction and land development standards. Most left them basically unchanged, 48 banks or 78.7 percent. Another 13.1 percent tightened somewhat and 8.2 percent eased somewhat.

Demand moved the other way. Of 60 banks, 21.7 percent reported weaker demand, while only 6 reported stronger demand.

Bank appetite is one input a lender can watch alongside local deal flow.

posts.text:
A borrower stops paying on a $420,000 loan at 11 percent, and the loan heads to foreclosure. What does waiting cost the lender each month?

Lost interest: $420,000 x 11 percent / 12 = $3,850.
Property taxes: $5,400 / 12 = $450.
Insurance: $3,000 / 12 = $250.

That is $4,550 a month, or $36,400 over 8 months. Those inputs are illustrative.

ATTOM data reported by HousingWire put the Q2 2026 national average foreclosure at 563 days. At that average, the carry would run longer.

Lenders can add a carry estimate to their loss math before a loan goes bad.

posts.text:
What is a bridge loan actually bridging?

A bridge loan is short-term financing that covers a temporary gap in funding. In real estate, that gap can be a property that is not yet eligible for permanent financing.

Terms vary by lender. PNC describes a few months to one year as typical. Adventures in CRE says a few months to several years.

The exit matters as much as the gap. One source calls refinancing into a permanent loan the typical exit. Lenders can weigh the exit as heavily as the gap.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three cards in a row: the gap (property not yet eligible for permanent financing), the bridge (a short-term loan covering the temporary gap), and the exit (refinance into a permanent loan). Below, PNC cites a few months to one year; Adventures in CRE cites a few months to several years.

sources.quote: Also referred to as a mini-perm, in real estate a bridge loan is a short-term loan typically provided to developers and value-add real estate investors and is used to "bridge" periods during which the property is not eligible for permanent financing. The term of a bridge loan can be anywhere from a few months to several years. The typical exit strategy is to refinance into a permanent loan with a lower interest rate

posts.text:
How much could a $240,000 parcel of raw land support as a loan?

Federal interagency real estate lending guidelines list supervisory loan-to-value limits of 65 percent for raw land and 75 percent for land development. They say institutions should set internal limits that do not exceed these.

On $240,000, 65 percent is $156,000. At 75 percent it is $180,000, a $24,000 gap.

These guidelines address regulated institutions, and private lender limits vary by lender. Some lenders look at them as a reference point when sizing a land loan.

posts.text:
A lender holds $4,350,000 of loans. Not every loan will pay as agreed. How do banks account for that?

A loss reserve, called an allowance for credit losses in bank accounting, is an estimate of expected credit losses. The Federal Reserve says losses can be measured on a pool basis when loans share similar risk characteristics.

Illustrative: $2,900,000 at 1.2 percent is $34,800. $1,450,000 at 3.0 percent is $43,500. Together that is $78,300, or 1.8 percent of the book.

Historical loss information is generally a starting point, adjusted for current conditions.

posts.text:
A first lien of $270,000 on a $450,000 property is 60 percent LTV. Add a $63,000 second lien and the risk picture changes.

Combined LTV adds every loan balance on the property, then divides by its value: ($270,000 + $63,000) / $450,000 = 74 percent.

The first lender gets first dibs on sale proceeds, so the second lien is first to take a shortfall. If value drops 10 percent to $405,000, combined LTV rises to 82.2 percent.

Lenders can compute it before funding and again if value changes. Illustrative numbers.

posts.text:
Work that was never closed out with the city can follow a property into your loan file.

Three places it can show up:

Value. Appraisers may not be able to count an unpermitted addition as gross living area, even if the work looks high quality.

Insurance. Unpermitted additions may not be covered under a homeowner's policy.

Closing. When an open permit appears in city records, a lender may not know whether the work was completed properly, and may suspend the mortgage.

Checking permit records early can avoid last-minute surprises. Rules vary by state and lender.

Pending home sales fell 7.3% in September from August, and 11.3% from a year earlier, NAR reported on October 20, 2026.

A pending sale is a signed contract that has not closed. NAR says a sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing.

So fewer contracts now may mean fewer closings and payoffs in the months ahead. Illustrative: a $265,000 loan at 12% interest-only accrues $2,650 a month. Each month a sale slips is another $2,650 of interest the borrower carries.

Lenders can check exit timelines against current contract activity.

posts.text:
A foreclosure sale brings $305,000 on a $290,000 loan. Is the lender whole? Not necessarily.

Illustrative math:
Sale $305,000 less 8 percent selling costs = $280,600 net.
Owed: $290,000 balance + $19,000 accrued interest + $13,000 costs = $322,000.
Loss: $322,000 less $280,600 = $41,400.

Over the $290,000 balance, that is 14.3 percent loss severity.

Two studies of residential mortgages measure severity as net loss over unpaid balance, and some leave out lost interest. Without it, this loss is $22,400, or 7.7 percent.

Lenders can state which definition they use.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two bars for an illustrative foreclosure sale: the lender is owed $322,000 ($290,000 balance, $19,000 interest, $13,000 costs); the $305,000 sale nets $280,600 after 8 percent selling costs, leaving a $41,400 loss. Severity is 14.3 percent with lost interest, 7.7 percent without.

sources.title: Mortgage Loss Severities: What Keeps Them So High?
sources.quote: We define the loss severity rate as the total net loss divided by the UPB at liquidation, in which total net loss includes net sales losses (net sale proceeds minus UPB), and liquidation expenses offset by non-mortgage insurance (non-MI) recoveries. Selling expenses are subtracted from gross sales proceeds to derive net sale proceeds.

sources.title: Loss Severity on Residential Mortgages: Evidence from Freddie Mac's Newest Data
sources.quote: We calculate severity as the unpaid principal balance of the loan plus expenses, less the net sales proceeds, less recoveries from MI and other sources as a percentage of the unpaid principal balance. Some readers may note that we have not included lost interest in our calculation of severity.

posts.text:
A borrower can have enough cash to close and still be one bad month from trouble.

That is why lenders can look at post-closing liquidity: the liquid assets a borrower still has after the loan closes and all transaction costs are paid.

One SBA lending source says a borrower with zero liquidity after closing is a significantly higher default risk. Another says reserves show a borrower can keep paying while a property recovers from a vacancy.

Lenders can also check what counts. Gifts, unsecured borrowed funds and home equity generally do not. Requirements depend on the loan program.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three step cards: liquid assets before the deal, close the loan and pay all costs, cash left is post-closing liquidity. Below, a note that reserves show a borrower can keep paying while a property recovers, and that gifts, unsecured borrowed funds and home equity generally do not count.

sources.quote: liquid assets a borrower will have remaining after the loan closes and all transaction costs are paid. From the lender's perspective, a borrower with zero liquidity after closing is a significantly higher default risk.

sources.title: How to Meet DSCR Reserve Requirements Without Draining Cash
sources.quote: Rent can dip. A tenant can leave. Reserves show you can keep paying while the property recovers. Gifts, unsecured borrowed funds, and home equity generally do not count.

posts.text:
A $900,000 loan is secured by 4 lots, each valued at $300,000. One lot sells. What must be paid down to release it?

Pro rata is $225,000, or 900,000 divided by 4. The price can be set higher. At 120 percent of the allocated amount, it is $270,000.

The remaining $630,000 loan then sits on 3 lots worth $900,000, or 70 percent loan to value. Pro rata would leave $675,000 against $900,000, or 75 percent.

One legal glossary cited by a lender site describes release prices of about 110 to 125 percent. Terms vary by lender.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two cards compare releasing one lot from a $900,000 loan on 4 lots worth $300,000 each. Pro rata release pays down $225,000, leaving $675,000 on $900,000 of value, 75 percent. A 120 percent release pays $270,000, leaving $630,000, 70 percent.

posts.text:
A lender sells part of a loan to an investor. Is that a participation or assignment? The answer decides who the borrower deals with.

In a participation, the lead lender keeps title to the loan, stays the borrower contact and manages servicing. The buyer is not a creditor of the borrower and cannot act against the borrower or collateral independently.

In an assignment, the entire note changes hands. The buyer replaces the seller as lender.

Before buying or selling, lenders can confirm with counsel who holds title, who services and who can enforce. Terms vary by agreement.
posts.alt: Comparison graphic of participation versus assignment. In a participation the lead lender keeps title, stays the borrower contact and manages servicing, and the buyer is not a creditor of the borrower. In an assignment the entire note changes hands and the buyer replaces the seller as lender.

sources.quote: Once the loan is funded, the lead lender manages all servicing functions. | Participants cannot independently pursue the borrower, file liens, or take legal action against the collateral. | Unlike a loan assignment, where the entire note changes hands, a participation preserves the lead lender's position as the sole point of contact with the borrower.

posts.text:
A borrower's hazard insurance lapses. What can the lender do?

Loan documents can let the lender buy coverage and charge the borrower. That is force-placed insurance, also called lender-placed. It may protect the lender more than the borrower, may omit personal property and liability coverage, and often costs more than a standard policy.

For covered home mortgages, federal servicing rules require written notice at least 45 days before a charge, and cancellation within 15 days of proof of coverage. Terms vary, and business-purpose loans may fall outside those rules.

Lenders can request renewal proof before a lapse.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Navy graphic titled Borrower insurance lapses. What can the lender do? Three steps for covered home mortgages: coverage lapses, written notice 45 days or more before a charge, and cancellation within 15 days of proof of coverage. Three cards say a force-placed policy may protect the lender more, may omit personal property and liability, and can cost much more.

sources.title: Force-Placed & Lender Placed Insurance
sources.quote: Force-placed insurance happens when your mortgage company or auto lender purchases an insurance policy on your vehicle or home. It may protect the lender more than you, may be missing coverages that protect you, like personal property and liability coverage, and can be much more expensive than a regular policy. Your lender is legally required to cancel your force-placed insurance within 15 days.

posts.text:
Same default, two different documents. What the lender holds can change the foreclosure path.

A mortgage is a two-party arrangement: borrower and lender. A mortgage foreclosure most often occurs judicially, which means it is filed in a court.

A deed of trust is a three-party arrangement. A trustee holds title for the lender until the loan is repaid, and a power-of-sale clause can allow a nonjudicial foreclosure with no court oversight.

Which instrument is used, and how it is enforced, varies by state. Lenders can confirm both before funding in a new state.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two comparison cards. Mortgage: two parties, borrower and lender; foreclosure most often judicial, filed in a court. Deed of trust: three parties, borrower, lender and trustee; foreclosure often nonjudicial under a power-of-sale clause. A panel notes this varies by state.

sources.title: Deed of Trust vs. Mortgage: What Private Lenders Need to Know
sources.quote: A mortgage is a two-party arrangement. A deed of trust is a three-party arrangement. In practice, the state where the collateral is located determines which instrument is recognized and how it is enforced.

sources.title: Deed of Trust vs Mortgage: What's the Difference
sources.quote: Foreclosure of a mortgage most often occurs judicially—this means it is filed in a court of law. Foreclosure of a deed of trust is often completed non-judicially, which means the court is not involved.

sources.title: What Is a Power of Sale Foreclosure?
sources.quote: With a power of sale foreclosure, also called a "nonjudicial" foreclosure, the lender can foreclose without court oversight. Each state has its own requirements.

Illustrative: a $241,000 flip with a $57,500 rehab budget. The loan is 85 percent of purchase plus 100 percent of rehab, or $262,350. Loan to cost: $262,350 / $298,500, about 87.9 percent.

Then the rehab runs $14,500 over. Total cost is now $313,000.

If the lender funds the overrun, the loan becomes $276,850 and LTC rises to 88.5 percent. If the borrower pays it, the loan stays $262,350 and LTC falls to 83.8 percent.

Lenders can decide who covers an overrun before approving a change.

posts.text:
When should a lender stop counting interest as income?

One bank call report criterion treats an asset as nonaccrual when principal or interest has been in default 90 days or more, unless it is both well secured and in the process of collection. Accounting guidance also says accrual is generally suspended when collecting interest is less than probable.

Illustrative: a $192,000 loan at 9.25 percent interest only earns $1,480 a month. Three unpaid months is $4,440 that may show as income but is not cash. Private lenders can check how investor reports label it. Not accounting advice.

posts.text:
A subcontractor the lender never hired sends a preliminary notice. Now what?

In some states, subs and suppliers send one to protect lien rights. In California it is due within 20 days of first furnishing work, and the construction lender is among the recipients. Nevada covers work in the 31 days before the notice. Rules vary by state.

One approach: a lender can log the arrival date, compare the sender to the names on draw requests, and ask the borrower whether that party is under contract.

A notice preserves the sender's lien rights.

posts.text:
A borrower loses a lawsuit before your loan closes. Does that judgment now sit on the property you are lending against?

It depends on the state. In Texas, a recorded and indexed abstract of judgment constitutes a lien on and attaches to the defendant's real property, including property acquired after recording. In Missouri's covered counties, no judgment is a lien on real estate until an abstract is entered in a record, and those liens rank by the sequence of entry.

Lenders can search county records for judgments against a borrower and ask a title professional how local law ranks them.

sources.quote: No judgment hereafter rendered by any court shall be a lien on real estate ... until an abstract of the judgment shall be entered in a record ... shall have priority according to the sequence of and from the time of its respective entry into the record

A lender compares two loan requests. Property A has $96,000 of NOI on a $1,200,000 loan. Property B has $84,000 on $1,000,000. Which has more income behind each dollar lent?

Debt yield is net operating income divided by the loan amount. A is 8 percent. B is 8.4 percent, so B has the higher debt yield despite less NOI.

Unlike DSCR, it uses no interest rate or amortization schedule. Unlike LTV, it uses no appraised value.

Lenders can read it alongside DSCR and LTV, since each ratio answers a different question.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two cards compare loan requests. Property A: NOI $96,000, loan $1,200,000, debt yield 8 percent. Property B: NOI $84,000, loan $1,000,000, debt yield 8.4 percent. Below, DSCR depends on rate and amortization, LTV on appraised value, debt yield only on NOI and loan amount.

sources.title: What is Debt Yield
sources.quote: Debt yield is the property's net operating income divided by the loan amount, expressed as a percentage. Unlike DSCR (which depends on the interest rate and amortization schedule) and LTV (which depends on the appraised value), debt yield depends only on two property-specific numbers: NOI and loan amount.

sources.title: Debt Yield
sources.quote: The debt yield is unique, however, because the metric is independent of fluctuating interest rates and real estate market values and is unaffected by the borrowing term, i.e. length of the loan amortization schedule.

A foreclosure sale is on the calendar. Then the borrower files for bankruptcy. What happens?

The U.S. Courts glossary calls the automatic stay an injunction that usually comes into force automatically when a bankruptcy case is filed. It stops actions such as foreclosures against the debtor and property of the bankruptcy estate.

One law firm says it takes effect without notice to creditors. One court lists common reasons to seek relief: the debtor is behind on payments, or there is no equity.

Questions about a bankruptcy filing are for the lender's attorney.

sources.title: Automatic stay (glossary of legal terms)
sources.quote: An injunction that usually comes into force automatically when a bankruptcy case is filed. This stops actions such as lawsuits, foreclosures, garnishments, and most collection activities against the debtor and property of the bankruptcy estate.

posts.text:
A home sells at a foreclosure sale for $410,000. The first lien is $330,000. Where does the other $80,000 go?

One source lists the order as sale expenses, the mortgage being foreclosed, junior liens in priority order, then the owner if anything remains. That source adds that each category is paid in full before the next. Surplus rules vary by state.

Illustrative: $410,000 less $12,000 costs leaves $398,000. The first lien takes $330,000, leaving $68,000. The $60,000 second lien is paid, leaving $8,000 for the owner.

Takeaway: lenders can run this waterfall before counting on a sale price.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Four bars show a $410,000 foreclosure sale paid in order: $12,000 sale costs leaves $398,000; $330,000 first lien leaves $68,000; $60,000 second lien leaves $8,000; the last $8,000 goes to the owner. Illustrative example.

sources.title: Real Property Quick Tip: How to Distribute Foreclosure Sale Proceeds
sources.quote: When property is sold at a foreclosure sale, the proceeds from that sale are distributed in the following order of priority: Expenses from the sale (e.g., attorney's fees, court costs); Mortgage being foreclosed; Junior liens, in order of lien priority; Debtor, if any surplus remains. The amount owed in each category must be completely paid off before the proceeds can be used to pay off the next category.

sources.title: How to Claim Foreclosure Surplus Funds
sources.quote: The laws that govern foreclosure surplus funds vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. (Also: Then, any excess proceeds left over after paying off these liens belong to the former homeowner. Page undated, accessed 2026-11-01.)

sources.title: Where Do Surplus Proceeds from a Foreclosure Sale Go?
sources.quote: The Code of Civil Procedure spells it out. (California order: foreclosure costs, then the foreclosing lender's secured loan, then junior lienors by priority, then any remainder to the owner.)

posts.text:
What does a wraparound mortgage do to your lien position?

The seller keeps the existing mortgage in place. The buyer pays the seller each month, and the seller pays the original lender.

The wrap loan sits behind the original mortgage in second, or junior, lien position. That adds two risks. If the seller stops paying, the original lender can foreclose even when the buyer pays on time. And a due-on-sale clause may let that lender demand full repayment.

Lenders can confirm who pays the underlying loan before relying on a wrap.
